name: Worldview
tagline: NASA's satellite pictures of the whole Earth, every day since 2000 — and the map is still there on a plane.
description:
No account, no install, no server between you and the imagery — and the one thing the original cannot do: this works with the connection off. NASA's Blue Marble, the coastlines, the borders and 1,240 searchable places are packed inside this file, so the Earth is on screen before anything has loaded, and every tile you have already looked at is still there in the air, in a tunnel, in a field. Hand someone the GIF and they open the exact day and place you left it on, with your layers and your saved views inside it. Press Invite and a colleague is on the same map, live, with their cursor on it — no link to paste, no room to set up.

What it is: a browser for NASA's Global Imagery Browse Services, the archive behind NASA Worldview. 74 layers — true colour from Terra, Aqua and VIIRS, fires and thermal anomalies, sea surface temperature, aerosols, night lights, snow, sea ice, precipitation, vegetation, land cover — most of it within three hours of the satellite passing overhead, and going back to 2000 for MODIS and 1981 for sea surface temperature.

Drag the timeline to scrub the date, or open a calendar that greys out the days the layer you are looking at does not publish. Stack layers, drag them into order, fade them into each other. Split the screen and put one day beside another. Press play and watch a hurricane turn, a lake disappear over twenty summers, or smoke cross an ocean — then save that animation as a GIF, encoded here on your device, every frame stamped with its date.

When a layer shows nothing, it says why: no record on this day, or nothing over this view. Legends come from NASA's own colour maps, never from a guess.

An independent, unofficial port. Imagery: NASA EOSDIS GIBS. Not endorsed by NASA.
